title: self-hosted-inference-battleground-brief
content:
One-line summary:
Redwood positioning brief for competing against self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and custom builds). Focus: concise messaging, win/loss patterns, build-vs-buy decision heuristics, and sales playbook for POCs.

Purpose:
- Give sales and product marketing a compact reference to articulate Redwood's advantages versus customers considering self-hosting.
- Provide repeatable objections -> rebuttals and a checklist for evaluating build vs buy economics and risk.

TL;DR (for quick use in calls):
- If your priority is predictable latency, accountability (SLA), and fast time-to-production without hiring a specialized ops team, Redwood is usually the faster route than vLLM/TGI/TensorRT DIY stacks.
- Self-hosted can win on raw unit cost for extremely stable, high-volume workloads if you already have infra + operator expertise.
- Redwood reduces risk (fallbacks, autoscaling, observability, rollouts) and accelerates product iteration — communicate with concrete failure modes and time-to-recovery examples.

Competitive snapshot (short cards):
1) vLLM / custom OSS runtime stacks
  - Strengths: Low-level control, active OSS community, fits teams wanting to own everything. Good for experiment-heavy research environments.
  - Weaknesses: Requires SRE/infra expertise, KV-cache and batching tuning, uncertain performance across model variants and long-tail prompts, limited commercial support.
  - Customer signals: Hiring of multiple infra ML engineers, repo forks, in-house optimizations.
  - How Redwood counters: Offer dedicated capacity + migration templates, emphasize reduced time-to-1st-production and fewer post-deploy incidents.

2) Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (TGI)
  - Strengths: Well-integrated with HF ecosystem, simple for teams already on HF; good defaults.
  - Weaknesses: Scaling beyond single-region clusters, versioning and rollouts, enterprise-grade observability and quotas are limited.
  - Customer signals: Heavy HF model usage, HF Hub reliance, or TGI deployed as first-step in infra.
  - Redwood counters: Highlight rollout controls, per-route cost/latency analytics, and model cataloging (pin + audit).

3) NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM and optimized vendor stacks
  - Strengths: Best-in-class kernel performance on supported hardware; strong for latency-sensitive, high-throughput inference.
  - Weaknesses: Hardware lock-in, engineering effort to support model families, complex quantization/compatibility issues, limited multi-cloud fit.
  - Customer signals: Dedicated on-prem GPU purchases, close NVIDIA partnership discussions.
  - Redwood counters: Emphasize smart routing across hardware tiers, model variant fallbacks, and cross-region resilience while showing comparable latencies at predictable costs.

4) Pure cloud-GPU + Triton or homegrown endpoint orchestration
  - Strengths: Maximum flexibility, control over infra and security.
  - Weaknesses: Operational burden, brittle autoscaling, unpredictable per-token costs without batching/kv-caching logic.
  - Redwood counters: Show how automatic batching/caching reduces token spend and latency variance vs DIY.

Build vs Buy decision framework (for customers):
- People: How many FTEs required to reach production (SRE + ML infra + reliability engineers)? If >3 full-time engineers just to keep endpoints stable, leaning buy.
- Pace: Time-to-POC and time-to-1st-customer. Self-hosted: weeks-to-months (often months). Redwood: days-to-weeks for a meaningful POC.
- Cost: Include hardware depreciation, egress, engineering salary, incident costs. Provide a simple 12–24 month TCO heuristic: if expected sustained QPS requires >10 dedicated GPUs, DIY might be cheaper at scale; otherwise managed wins.
- Risk: Compliance, DR, and security — does the team have KMS/HSM policies and audit log requirements? If yes, Redwood Private can be quicker than building these controls in-house.
- Velocity & feature shipping: Can your team tolerate outages/rollbacks? If not, buy.

Practical break-even heuristics to share on calls:
- Small startups / feature teams: <5M tokens/month: buy almost always — engineering tax dominates.
- Growing product teams: 5M–50M tokens/month: depends on hiring pipeline and SRE maturity; Redwood Dedicated often cheaper when factoring ops.
- Hyper-scale customers: >50M+ tokens/month with predictable patterns and in-house GPU ops: self-hosted/TensorRT might be cost-effective.

Common buyer objections & suggested rebuttals (short):
- "We want full control over the stack." -> Rebuttal: "We provide model pinning, private deploys, and observability so you retain control without 3x ops overhead. See migration checklist for how control is preserved."
- "Managed is more expensive." -> Rebuttal: "Measured TCO includes incident response, developer uptime, and time-to-market. We can run a 30-day POC and side-by-side cost comparison using your workload traces."
- "We need absolute lowest latency." -> Rebuttal: "We benchmark on target hardware and provide Dedicated with SLAs and routing to optimal kernels; we also support on‑prem private deployment if hardware locality is required."
- "We already invested in vLLM/TGI proof-of-concept." -> Rebuttal: "Great — Redwood can import configs and run a canary period with mirrored traffic; we focus on stabilizing and reducing ops load so your engineers can move to product work."

Sales playbook / POC checklist (quick):
1) Collect sample workload (traces, prompt lengths, concurrency) and security requirements.
2) Run Redwood hosted benchmark using customer traces (3 days).
3) Offer Dedicated trial or Private trial for customers with strict compliance (2–4 weeks).
4) Success criteria: 95th pct latency target met, token-unit cost within agreed threshold, zero-severity incidents requiring customer infra changes.

Messaging by buyer profile:
- AI-native startups: Emphasize fast iteration, SDKs, low friction, and cost optimization (Optimize recommendations).
- Enterprise product teams: Emphasize SLAs, audit logs, private deployments, and predictable capacity.
- Platform teams: Emphasize standardization, routing policies, rollout controls, and multi-model catalog.

Suggested collateral to build quickly:
- Side-by-side TCO spreadsheet template (fill with customer numbers).
- A short 'migration playbook' doc that maps vLLM/TGI/TensorRT components to Redwood features.
- Benchmarking repo with sample traces and reproducible scripts (GH link above).
- One-pager battlecard per competitor with heartbeat signals to listen for in discovery calls.

Next actions (owners + due dates):
- Draft TCO spreadsheet template: Avi Patel — due 2026-01-30.
- Migration playbook draft (vLLM -> Redwood): Sofia Martinez — due 2026-02-10.
- Create one-pager competitor battlecards (HF/TGI, vLLM, TensorRT): Maya Chen — due 2026-01-25.

Notes & open questions:
- We need better public numbers for TensorRT-LLM latencies on <context=2048> for Llama2-70B quantized; engineering to surface internal benchmarks.
- Consider an internal DR scenario doc demonstrating fallback behaviors between Dedicated and Hosted for sales demos.

Tone: conversational, practical, with concrete playbook steps. Use this doc as living guidance; update after 3 POCs to capture real-world win/loss signals.

End of brief.
